prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Tencent Music Entertainment Group" (ticker TME), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "TME", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Tencent Music Entertainment Group
result.industry: Online music and audio streaming and entertainment (China)
markets: Music streaming subscriptions in China (QQ Music, Kugou Music, Kuwo Music)
Music-related advertising, artist and IP services, concerts and merchandise
Online karaoke and music live-streaming social entertainment (WeSing, Kugou/Kuwo live rooms)
Long-form audio: audiobooks and podcasts (Ximalaya, acquired May 2026)

mission.statement: TME's mission is to create endless possibilities with music and technology.
mission.source: 'About Tencent Music Entertainment' section of the company's Q2 2026 earnings release (Form 6-K, August 2026)
mission.plain: Use technology to give people new and better ways to enjoy and make music.

about.plain: Tencent Music runs China's biggest music apps, QQ Music, Kugou Music and Kuwo Music, plus the karaoke app WeSing and, since May 2026, the audiobook and podcast app Ximalaya. People can listen for free with ads or pay a monthly fee for more songs, better sound and extra perks. It also earns money from ads, from fans buying virtual gifts for singers in live shows, and from concerts and fan merchandise. It is controlled by the internet giant Tencent.
about.customers: Hundreds of millions of Chinese music listeners, of whom about 127 million paid for a music subscription at the end of 2025, plus advertisers and artists.
about.everyday: It is like Spotify for China, built into the same Tencent world as the WeChat messaging app.

money.plain: monthly paid plans for music apps, including the premium SVIP tier (shares are H1 2026)
ads, artist promotion, concerts, merchandise and digital albums
virtual gifts in karaoke and music live-streaming shows
audiobook and podcast subscriptions and ads, added in May 2026
concert tours, fan meetings and artist merchandise
AI DJ, AI singing and creation features and AI agents in Weixin

result.summary: Tencent Music has a real but weakening advantage: the deepest licensed music catalogue in China, two of the three most-used music apps and deep ties to Tencent's WeChat and QQ give it scale no rival matches, and it has turned that into gross margins that rose from 31.9% in 2020 to 44.2% in 2025. However, ByteDance's free, Douyin-fed Soda Music grew to about 156 million monthly users by March 2026, regulators have barred exclusive licensing, and TME's own music user count fell 5% in 2025, so the moat is being tested.

pricingPower.evidence: Monthly music ARPPU rose from RMB11.1 in Q4 2024 to RMB11.9 in Q4 2025 while paying users still grew from 121.0 million to 127.4 million and SVIP subscribers passed 20 million, but membership revenue growth slowed to 8.1% in Q2 2026 and the CEO said price-sensitive Kugou users were 'easily flowing away' to free rivals.

moats.evidence: QQ Music and Kugou are household names in China with the deepest licensed catalogue from the major labels, but brands matter less than catalogue and price for many users, as Soda Music's rise shows.

Playlists, listening history and SVIP perks create some stickiness, but songs are widely available elsewhere and users can try free rivals easily; TME's music MAUs fell from 556 million to 528 million in 2025.
Integration with Tencent's QQ and Weixin social graph and community features (comments, karaoke, live rooms) add value as more people use them, though music listening itself has weak network effects.

With RMB32.9 billion of 2025 revenue versus NetEase Cloud Music's RMB7.8 billion, TME spreads licensing and technology costs over a far larger paying base, earning a 44.2% gross margin versus NetEase Cloud Music's 35.7%.
Licensing deals with all major labels and the cost of a full catalogue limit the market to a few platforms, though ByteDance has shown deep-pocketed entrants can still break in.
TME is the incumbent; it is the free, traffic-led Soda Music model that counter-positions against TME's paid-membership approach.
Long experience converting free users to paid tiers (SVIP above 20 million in 2025) and running IP-led offline events and artist services is hard to copy quickly.

Exclusive licensing was banned by China's regulator in 2021 and the May 2026 Ximalaya approval added a ban on new exclusive audio licences, so content access is no longer cornered, although self-owned and artist-partnership IP is growing.

customers.evidence: Paying music users grew to 127.4 million in Q4 2025 and SVIP passed 20 million, but online music MAUs fell 5% year on year to 528 million and management cited users leaving for free rivals in Q1 2026; no NPS is published.

talent.evidence: As a Tencent subsidiary TME draws on Tencent's engineering pool and reputation (CEO Ross Liang is a 20-year Tencent veteran), but TME itself does not appear in published employer rankings.

product.evidence: QQ Music and Kugou are China's two most-used music apps (about 201 million and 205 million MAUs in March 2026, QuestMobile) with the broadest licensed catalogue and features such as AI DJ, but rivals compete on free access and recommendation quality.

competitors.name: NetEase Cloud Music
competitors.note: Number-two paid music streaming platform in China; competes for subscribers, young users and independent artists.

competitors.name: ByteDance (Soda Music / Qishui Yinyue, Douyin)
competitors.note: Free, ad-supported Soda Music fed by Douyin traffic reached about 156 million MAUs in March 2026; Douyin also competes for music discovery and live-streaming gifts.

competitors.name: Kuaishou Technology
competitors.note: Short-video and live-streaming platform competing for user time, music discovery and virtual-gift spending.

competitors.name: Bilibili Inc.
competitors.note: Video community with music content, live streaming and young users.

competitors.name: China Mobile (Migu Music)
competitors.note: Migu Music streaming bundled with mobile plans.

competitors.name: Huawei (Huawei Music)
competitors.note: Pre-installed music app on Huawei phones.

competitors.name: Apple Inc. (Apple Music)
competitors.note: Paid streaming service on iPhones in China.

competitors.name: HUYA Inc.
competitors.note: Live-streaming platform competing for virtual-gift spending and streamers.

competitors.name: DouYu International Holdings
competitors.note: Live-streaming platform competing for virtual-gift spending.

competitors.name: Spotify Technology
competitors.note: Global streaming leader; not operating in mainland China but competes for label deals and in some overseas markets (TME holds a stake in Spotify).

estimates.name: NetEase Cloud Music (not an SEC filer; HKEX-reported figures, converted at RMB6.9931/US$)
Kuaishou Technology (estimate, FY2024; not an SEC filer)

marketShare.market: China music streaming apps (share of combined monthly active users of the four largest apps; Kuwo not included)

threats: ByteDance's free Soda Music, fed by Douyin traffic, reached about 156 million MAUs by March 2026 and is pulling price-sensitive users away from Kugou
Falling user base: TME music MAUs dropped from 556 million to 528 million in 2025, and TME stopped reporting quarterly MAU, paying-user and ARPPU figures in 2026

Regulation: China's SAMR banned exclusive music licensing in 2021 and attached five conditions to the May 2026 Ximalaya approval, including no new exclusive audio licences and no bundling for automakers
AI-generated music and 'song-washing' copies diluting the value of licensed catalogues
Shrinking social-entertainment revenue (down 16.4% year on year in Q2 2026)
Integration risk and higher debt from the cash-and-stock Ximalaya acquisition (borrowings of RMB13.1 billion at June 30, 2026, up from none at end-2025)
US-China tensions and the risk of US delisting rules for Chinese ADRs

ceo.name: Ross Liang (Liang Zhu)
ceo.background: PhD in signal and information processing (Tianjin University, 2003); formerly at Huawei; joined Tencent in 2003, ran QQ Music 2014-2016 and became a Tencent vice president in 2016

c1.evidence: TME leads China's music streaming market with QQ Music and Kugou, but the industry is maturing: revenue grew only 5.1% a year from 2022 to 2025 and 5.8% in Q2 2026.

c2.evidence: Users pick TME for the broadest licensed catalogue and Tencent/Weixin integration, but exclusive licensing is banned and free Soda Music is winning users, so the edge is copyable.

c3.evidence: QQ Music and Kugou are household names and the default music apps in China (about 201 million and 205 million MAUs in March 2026), but the TME name itself is little known outside China.

c4.evidence: The mission 'to create endless possibilities with music and technology' appears in each earnings release, but management communication focuses mostly on revenue, margins and buybacks.

c6.evidence: “QQ Music, Tencent, paid music” - mostly neutral-to-positive in China as a reliable default, while investors now associate it with slowing growth and competition from ByteDance.

c7.evidence: China's paid music market is large (TME alone had 127.4 million paying users in 2025) and still underpaid versus the West, but it is not a fast-growing secular trend; consensus sees about 7% annual revenue growth to 2028.

c8.evidence: TME is expanding into long-form audio (Ximalaya, May 2026), concerts, merchandise and AI music tools, though all remain within China's audio entertainment market.

m1.evidence: Ross Liang talks of a 'content-and-platform' strategy and AI-powered music, but has not set out a distinctive long-range vision beyond China audio entertainment.

m2.evidence: Ross Liang is a professional Tencent executive appointed CEO in April 2021, not a founder.

m4.evidence: There is no public evidence either way of a servant-leadership style at TME.

m5.evidence: Under Liang TME launched SVIP, AI DJ and AI creation tools and offline IP events, but the culture is largely Tencent's rather than distinctively built by the CEO.

m6.evidence: Liang holds a PhD in signal and information processing and previously ran QQ Music's product as general manager (2014-2016).

m7.evidence: No public record suggests either unusual character or controversy; stewardship is aimed at shareholders and Tencent.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Ross Liang giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Liang keeps a low public profile and is not known for a distinctive public persona.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in 2021, gross margin rose from 30.1% (2021) to 44.2% (2025) and net profit attributable rose from RMB3.0 billion to RMB11.1 billion, though users fell in 2025.

m10.evidence: TME cut operating costs as a share of revenue and grew margins sharply since 2021, but there is no particular reputation for frugality.

c10.evidence: TME's apps give hundreds of millions of people in China legal access to music, but its reach is almost entirely limited to China.

p2.evidence: Running a licensed music streaming service is valuable but not technically extremely hard, as ByteDance's fast-growing Soda Music shows.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose in 2021 and 2024-2025 but fell in 2022 (RMB28.3bn) and 2023 (RMB27.8bn) from RMB31.2bn in 2021.

f2.evidence: Gross margin rose from 31.9% in 2020 to 44.2% in 2025 and operating margin from 16.2% to 40.6% (2025 includes one-off other gains).

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 cash, term deposits and short-term investments of RMB44.2 billion exceeded borrowings and notes of RMB16.5 billion, and equity was RMB81.1 billion.

f4.evidence: Operating profit rose from RMB4.7 billion (2020) to RMB13.4 billion (2025) and operating cash flow from RMB4.9 billion to RMB10.2 billion, though with dips in 2021 and 2023.

v1.evidence: QQ Music and Kugou offer China's broadest licensed catalogue, but NetEase Cloud Music (community) and Soda Music (free) give users good reasons to choose them instead.

v2.evidence: TME does not appear in published best-employer rankings; parent Tencent is regarded as a top employer in China.

c5.evidence: Hundreds of millions of Chinese listeners, singers and artists who rely on QQ Music, Kugou and WeSing would miss it, though rivals could replace much of it.
